title: The Heavenly Twins
description: Published in 1893 and the central English New Woman novel: the twin boys Angelica and Diavolo and the destruction of women by the marriage market.
plot_or_argument: Evadne Frayling, married to a man diseased by his past, refuses to consummate the marriage and dedicates herself to reform; Angelica Hamilton-Wells, married in her teens to a middle-aged general, educates herself in secret and finally runs away to live with the cross-dressing page Tenor; the twin brothers and their tutor provide the novel's comedy, and Edith Beale's death from inherited syphilis provides its indictment.
historical_context: 1890-93: the Contagious Diseases Acts campaign, the sexual ignorance of middle-class girls, the marriage law and the feminist periodicals of the early 1890s.
literary_significance: The Heavenly Twins was the most discussed novel of 1893 and it made the New Woman a national figure: its treatment of venereal disease, sexual ignorance and the double standard made it a founding text of the English feminist novel, and the phrase 'the New Woman' entered the language from its pages and its reviews.

title: The Beth Book
description: Published in 1897 and Grand's finest novel: the growth of a girl of genius into an independent woman against every obstacle of Victorian family life.
plot_or_argument: Beth Caldwell grows up in an Irish and English household of careless parents and brutal schooling, marries a young doctor who proves to be drunken and tyrannical, and after years of illness and poverty discovers her vocation as a writer and an orator for women's freedom.
historical_context: 1896-97: the Irish and English provincial middle class, the Victorian education of girls, and the feminist lecture platform of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Beth Book is the most fully realised of the New Woman novels and one of the first English novels to treat a woman's artistic vocation from childhood to fulfilment: its portrait of a girl of genius has made it a key text in the history of women's writing.

title: Ideala
description: Published in 1888 and the first of Grand's novels of the woman question: the spiritual history of a wife who cannot accept the double standard.
plot_or_argument: Ideala, a beautiful and spiritual woman unhappily married to a dull and selfish husband, travels through Europe in search of faith and freedom, refuses the love of a good man rather than break the marriage law, and finds at last a vocation of social work among the poor.
historical_context: 1887-88: the Victorian debate on marriage and divorce, the higher education of women, and the spiritual crisis of the 1880s.
literary_significance: Ideala was the first of the New Woman novels and a founding text of the genre: its heroine's refusal of the double standard and her search for a life of her own made it a book that Victorian women read as a manifesto.

title: The New Aspect of the Woman Question
description: Published in March 1894 and the essay that named the movement: Grand's statement of what the New Woman wanted and why.
plot_or_argument: Grand argues that the woman movement is a claim for the 'new aspect' of an old question: women demand education, economic independence and a single moral standard, and they claim the right to be judged as individuals rather than as members of a sex, in an essay that answers the caricatures of the New Woman in the press.
historical_context: 1894: the North American Review's symposium on the woman question, the suffrage campaigns, and the height of the New Woman controversy in Britain and America.
literary_significance: 'The New Aspect of the Woman Question' is the manifesto of the New Woman and one of the most influential feminist essays of the century: it defined the movement for its contemporaries, it was reprinted and answered across the English-speaking world, and it remains the clearest statement of what the 1890s meant by the New Woman.

title: 'Marriage' (1888)
description: Published in August 1888 and the essay that provoked the greatest marriage debate of the century: an argument against the indissolubility of marriage.
plot_or_argument: 'Marriage' argues that the legal indissolubility of marriage makes the wife a chattel, that the double standard is enforced by law, that many marriages are legalised prostitution, and that women must be free to leave intolerable unions; the essay calls for equal divorce, for the economic independence of wives and for a single moral standard.
historical_context: 1888: the Westminster Review, the campaign for the custody of children and the Married Women's Property Acts, and the periodical press of the late 1880s.
literary_significance: 'Marriage' is a founding document of English feminism and the most radical Victorian argument on marriage: it drew over 27,000 replies in the periodical press, it made Caird the most notorious woman in England, and it set the agenda of the New Woman novel for the next decade.

title: The Daughters of Danaus
description: Published in 1894 and the most intellectually ambitious New Woman novel: the sacrifice of a woman composer to her family and the maternal 'instinct'.
plot_or_argument: Hadria Fullerton, a gifted composer, is urged by her family to marry and to give up her music for husband and children; she marries, bears children she cannot love, struggles to compose in secret, and finally leaves her husband to live alone and work, in a novel that refuses the conventional reconciliation.
historical_context: 1892-94: the debate on the 'maternal instinct', the position of the woman artist, the campaign for the Married Women's Property Acts, and the feminist circles of the early 1890s.
literary_significance: The Daughters of Danaus is the most searching of the New Woman novels and the only one to make a woman artist's vocation its central subject: its refusal of the maternal ideal and its unflinching account of the cost of marriage made it the most radical feminist novel of the 1890s, and it has been recovered as a key text of Victorian feminism.

title: The Wing of Azrael
description: Published in 1889 and the first novel to dramatise Caird's argument against marriage: a wife's revolt against a brutal husband.
plot_or_argument: Viola Sedgwick is married to a man she has been persuaded to accept, and finds herself trapped in a union of legalised cruelty; she falls in love with another man, refuses to elope, and is driven to the edge of madness before her husband's death releases her.
historical_context: 1888-89: the agitation after 'Marriage', the divorce law of 1857, and the Victorian treatment of wives' insanity.
literary_significance: The Wing of Azrael is the first novel to put Caird's feminist argument into narrative form: its portrait of a wife's psychological destruction by marriage was one of the most shocking books of 1889 and it prepared the way for the New Woman fiction of the 1890s.

title: The Stones of Sacrifice
description: Published in 1915 and Caird's last novel: a study of heredity, education and the sacrifice demanded of women by the family.
plot_or_argument: A young woman of scientific mind is asked to give up her research to nurse the family that has stunted her; the novel examines heredity, the claims of the old and the young, and the ethics of self-sacrifice, and refuses the consolations of conventional piety.
historical_context: 1913-15: the science of heredity, the suffrage campaign at its height, and the pre-war debate on the family.
literary_significance: The Stones of Sacrifice is Caird's most concentrated late work and shows the continuity of the feminist argument into the twentieth century: it treats heredity and self-sacrifice with a scientific seriousness rare in fiction and it is an important bridge between Victorian and modern feminism.

title: Pelham; or, The Adventures of a Gentleman
description: Published in 1828 and the founding English 'silver-fork' novel: the education of a fashionable young gentleman in the world of London society.
plot_or_argument: Henry Pelham, a rich and elegant young man about town, is sent abroad as secretary to an embassy, becomes entangled in the murder of a gambler, clears himself by his own courage and intelligence, and returns to marry the woman he loves and to take up the political career that his fashionable idleness had postponed.
historical_context: 1828: the London season, the dandy culture of the 1820s, the new gentleman's clubs, and the vogue for the fashionable novel after Scott.
literary_significance: Pelham created the fashionable novel and the dandy hero of the 1830s: its picture of London society, its epigrams and its elegant, self-conscious narrator made it the model for Disraeli's novels and for Thackeray's satire, and its portrait of the gentleman as a man of style rather than birth was a decisive innovation in English fiction.

title: The Last Days of Pompeii
description: Published in 1834 and the most popular historical novel of the ancient world in English: the destruction of Pompeii in AD 79.
plot_or_argument: Glaucus, a young Athenian, loves Ione but is entangled with the Egyptian priest Arbaces and the blind flower-girl Nydia; the novel follows the intrigues of the pagan priesthood, the conversion of the lovers to Christianity, and the eruption of Vesuvius that buries the city and kills Arbaces.
historical_context: 1834: the excavations at Pompeii, the vogue for the classical historical novel after Scott, and the Victorian interest in the early Christians under Rome.
literary_significance: The Last Days of Pompeii is the most successful classical historical novel in English and the book that made Pompeii a household name: its reconstruction of Roman domestic life and its spectacular catastrophe set the pattern for the historical novel of antiquity, and it has been adapted for stage, opera and film more than any other English novel of the ancient world.

title: The Lady of Lyons; or, Love and Pride
description: First performed in 1838 and the most popular Victorian domestic drama: a poor gardener's son wins a great lady by a deception and must win her again by worth.
plot_or_argument: Claude Melnotte, a proud young gardener's son in Lyons, is tricked by Pauline Deschappelles's jilted suitor into a mock marriage with her; she believes it real, he confesses the deception, goes to the wars, returns a colonel, and wins her love in earnest in the last act.
historical_context: 1838: the Covent Garden and Drury Lane patent theatres, the romantic drama after the decline of the legitimate stage, and the Victorian cult of self-made worth.
literary_significance: The Lady of Lyons was one of the most performed plays of the nineteenth century and the classic Victorian drama of class and love: Macready's production made it a favourite of the English and American stage for fifty years, and it is the best surviving example of the romantic verse drama that filled the patent theatres.

title: The Coming Race
description: Published in 1871 and the first English scientific romance of a superior underground race: the discovery of a subterranean civilisation powered by a mysterious force.
plot_or_argument: An American mining engineer descends into a vast cavern and finds the Vril-ya, a race of winged superhuman beings who live in a socialist utopia powered by 'vril'; he learns their language and customs, is nearly married to a Vril-ya woman, and escapes back to the surface with a warning about the future of humanity.
historical_context: 1871: the Darwinian debate, the electrical and galvanic sciences, the utopian fiction of the 1870s, and the fear of a coming master race.
literary_significance: The Coming Race introduced the word 'vril' and founded the English scientific romance of a hidden superior civilisation: it anticipated H. G. Wells and the whole tradition of the scientific utopia and dystopia, and its vision of a technologically powered master race became one of the founding myths of modern popular fiction.

title: Zanoni
description: Published in 1842 and the founding English occult novel: the love of an immortal Rosicrucian for a young singer, and the price of immortality.
plot_or_argument: Zanoni, a Rosicrucian brother who has conquered death, loves Viola, a young opera singer; he must choose between his immortal wisdom and mortal love, and his pupil Glyndon is tempted by the powers that Zanoni renounces, in a novel that moves from Naples to Paris during the Revolution.
historical_context: 1842: the Rosicrucian revival, the Mesmerist and Swedenborgian circles of the 1840s, and the Victorian fascination with the occult.
literary_significance: Zanoni founded the English occult novel and the modern literature of the immortal adept: its combination of Rosicrucian lore, mesmerism and revolutionary history influenced Bulwer's friend Dickens, the theosophists, and the whole tradition of occult fiction from Rider Haggard to Dion Fortune.

title: The Caxtons: A Family Picture
description: Published in 1849 and Bulwer's gentlest and most successful family novel: the education of a young man by his bookish father and his practical uncle.
plot_or_argument: Pisistratus Caxton, the son of a scholarly country clergyman, is educated at home, sent to London, ruined by an early literary success, and finally settled by the plain good sense of his uncle Roland; the novel ends with the family reunited and the father's great book completed.
historical_context: 1849: the English country parsonage, the literary market of the 1840s, and the Victorian ideal of the family as a school of character.
literary_significance: The Caxtons was the most popular of Bulwer's domestic novels and one of the finest English family chronicles of the 1840s: its affectionate portrait of a bookish father and its comedy of literary ambition made it a great favourite, and it inaugurated the 'My Novel' series that carried the family story into the 1850s.

title: Coningsby; or, The New Generation
description: Published in 1844 and the first of the Young England novels: the education of a young aristocrat in the politics of his country.
plot_or_argument: Coningsby, the orphaned grandson of a Whig marquess, is educated at Eton and Cambridge, discovers the corruption of the party system, is disinherited and then restored by the discovery of a secret marriage, and marries the woman he loves while being elected to Parliament as the spokesman of a regenerated Toryism.
historical_context: 1844: the Young England movement, the Conservative split over Peel and the Corn Laws, the beginnings of the railway age, and the 1841 election.
literary_significance: Coningsby created the English political novel as a serious form: it is the first novel to analyse the machinery of party politics from inside, its portrait of Peel and of the political world is one of the sharpest pieces of satire in Victorian fiction, and it made the Young England idea a national talking point.

title: Sybil; or, The Two Nations
description: Published in 1845 and the most important English novel of the condition of England: the discovery of the two nations, rich and poor.
plot_or_argument: Charles Egremont, a young aristocrat, travels in the industrial north and discovers the misery of the mining and manufacturing districts; he falls in love with Sybil, the daughter of a Chartist leader, follows the Chartist petition and the Plug Plot riots of 1842, and at the end discovers that Sybil is the true heir of the landed estate that his own family had usurped.
historical_context: 1845: the Chartist petition of 1842, the Plug Plot riots, the reports of the Children's Employment Commission, the Anti-Corn Law agitation, and the Young England movement.
literary_significance: Sybil is the first English novel to make the industrial working class the central subject of national politics: its phrase 'the two nations' entered the language, its documentary account of the mining districts influenced Engels and the whole condition-of-England tradition, and it remains the most important political novel of the 1840s.

title: Tancred; or, The New Crusade
description: Published in 1847 and the strangest of the Young England trilogy: a young English aristocrat goes to Jerusalem and the Sinai to discover the meaning of faith.
plot_or_argument: Tancred, heir to the Duke of Bellamont, refuses a political career and travels to the Holy Land, where he meets the mysterious Fakredeen, journeys with him to the desert, encounters the Jewish scholar Sidonia and the beautiful Eva, and returns to England with a vision of a spiritual destiny for the English nation.
historical_context: 1847: the Eastern question, the beginnings of Zionism, the Victorian enthusiasm for the Holy Land, and the religious crisis of the 1840s.
literary_significance: Tancred is the most ambitious and most prophetic of Disraeli's novels: its portrait of Sidonia, its vision of a Jewish national destiny in Palestine, and its argument that the English aristocracy needs a spiritual mission made it a founding text of the Zionist imagination and one of the most extraordinary political romances of the century.

title: Lothair
description: Published in 1870 and Disraeli's most popular late novel: a rich young nobleman torn between the Catholic Church, the revolutionary party and the English constitution.
plot_or_argument: Lothair, an orphaned millionaire peer, is courted by the Roman Catholic party, by the Italian patriot Mazzini's revolutionaries and by his English guardians; he travels to Rome, to the battle of Mentana, and to the English country houses, and finally settles into an English marriage and an English political career.
historical_context: 1870: the Vatican Council and the doctrine of papal infallibility, the Italian Risorgimento, the Fenian troubles, and the year of the first Education Act.
literary_significance: Lothair was the best-selling novel of 1870 and the most discussed book of its year: its portraits of contemporary figures and its treatment of the Catholic question made it a sensation, and it is the best of Disraeli's late novels and a brilliant picture of the English ruling class in the age of Gladstone.

title: Endymion (Disraeli)
description: Published in 1880 and Disraeli's last completed novel: the rise of a young man of no family in London politics.
plot_or_argument: Endymion Ferrars, the son of a disgraced politician, is educated at Oxford, enters the diplomatic service, falls in love with the rich and beautiful Myra, and makes his way to the highest office through the drawing rooms, the clubs and the press of London.
historical_context: 1880: the London of the Reform Club and the great political hostesses, the Eastern crisis of 1876-78, and the world of the 'social politics' of the 1870s.
literary_significance: Endymion is the most finished of Disraeli's political novels and the best picture of the London political world of the 1870s: its portrait of a young man's rise through society is a masterly study of the relation between politics and the drawing room, and it forms a pair with Lothair as his testament to his own world.

title: Mrs Warren's Profession
description: Written in 1893 and the most notorious of Shaw's 'unpleasant' plays: a Cambridge graduate discovers that her mother's fortune comes from the brothels of Europe.
plot_or_argument: Vivie Warren, a brilliant young woman of the new generation, learns that her mother Kitty has made her money as a brothel-keeper, and that her own father is Sir George Crofts, the capitalist who invests in the trade; she refuses to be shocked, refuses to be sentimental, and leaves for London to live her own life, while her mother defends the choice as the only one open to a poor woman.
historical_context: 1893: the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, the debates over prostitution and the 'social evil', and the censorship of the Lord Chamberlain.
literary_significance: Mrs Warren's Profession was banned by the censor and not performed in public in Britain until 1925, and it remains the most powerful English play about prostitution: its argument that vice is an economic institution, not a moral failing, made it a founding text of modern social drama and the most radical of Shaw's early plays.

title: Arms and the Man
description: First performed in 1894 and Shaw's first great commercial success: a romantic young woman's illusions about war and love are destroyed by a practical Swiss soldier.
plot_or_argument: Raina Petkoff, a Bulgarian officer's daughter engaged to the heroic Sergius, shelters a Swiss mercenary, Captain Bluntschli, who carries chocolates instead of cartridges; the war ends, Bluntschli returns to recover his coat, and the play ends with Raina engaged to him and her romantic ideals entirely dismantled.
historical_context: 1894: the Serbo-Bulgarian war of 1885, the vogue of the heroic war play, and the New Woman's criticism of romantic love.
literary_significance: Arms and the Man is the play that made Shaw's reputation and the founding English anti-war comedy: its destruction of the romantic hero and its argument that the soldier's real business is survival had an enormous influence on the English theatre, and it remains one of the most performed of his plays.

title: Candida
description: Written in 1894 and performed in 1897: the most accomplished of Shaw's early plays, a comedy about a wife, a clergyman and the poet who loves her.
plot_or_argument: Candida Morell, the wife of a Christian Socialist clergyman, is loved by the young poet Eugene Marchbanks; she is forced to choose between them and chooses her husband, not out of weakness but because he is the weaker of the two and needs her, while the poet is left to go alone.
historical_context: 1894: the Christian Socialist movement, the New Woman debate, and the cult of the poet as the superior being.
literary_significance: Candida is the finest of Shaw's early comedies and one of the great English plays about marriage: its treatment of the wife as the strongest person in the house and its rejection of both the romantic and the sentimental view of love made it a classic of the modern stage.

title: Man and Superman
description: Published in 1903 and Shaw's masterpiece of ideas: the pursuit of a fugitive man by a woman determined to marry him, and the dream of Don Juan in hell.
plot_or_argument: Jack Tanner, a wealthy political theorist, is made guardian to Ann Whitefield, who decides to marry him; he flees to Spain with her and her mother in pursuit, is captured by brigands, dreams the third-act 'Don Juan in Hell' in which the Life Force is debated by Don Juan, the Devil and Doña Ana, and wakes to accept his destiny as Ann's husband.
literary_form: Play (four acts, with 'Don Juan in Hell' interlude)
historical_context: 1903: the Fabian Society, the Nietzschean philosophy of the superman, the debate on eugenics and the Life Force, and the New Woman's sexuality.
literary_significance: Man and Superman is the fullest statement of Shaw's philosophy and the central English play of ideas: its preface on the philosophic man, its dream interlude and its invention of the Shavian 'Life Force' made it one of the most influential plays of the twentieth century, and it brought the discussion play to its highest point.

title: Major Barbara
description: First performed in 1905 and the greatest of Shaw's plays about poverty: a Salvation Army major and her millionaire munitions-making father contest the right way to save souls.
plot_or_argument: Major Barbara Undershaft, an officer of the Salvation Army, is confronted by her father Andrew Undershaft, the armaments magnate who owns the souls of the town of Perivale St Andrews; the Army accepts his money, Barbara loses her faith in its methods, and she goes to the model town to convert the well-fed workers of the armaments factory.
historical_context: 1905: the Salvation Army, the Boer War and the armaments industry, the Fabian campaign against poverty, and the ethics of the 'tainted money' debate.
literary_significance: Major Barbara is the most complete of Shaw's social plays and one of the greatest English plays of the century: its argument that poverty is the worst of crimes and that the soul cannot be saved on an empty stomach made it a landmark of modern drama, and its first-act meeting of Barbara and Undershaft is one of the great scenes of English comedy.

title: Pygmalion
description: Written in 1912 and first performed in 1914: the flower-girl taught to speak like a duchess, and the professor of phonetics who cannot see what he has done.
plot_or_argument: Henry Higgins, a phonetician, bets Colonel Pickering that he can pass the Covent Garden flower-seller Eliza Doolittle off as a duchess in six months; she learns the accent and the manners, wins the ambassador's ball, and then confronts Higgins with the fact that he has made her a lady with no means of being one.
historical_context: 1912-14: the phonetic science of Henry Sweet, the class system of English speech, and the campaign for women's suffrage.
literary_significance: Pygmalion is Shaw's most popular play and one of the great English comedies: its use of phonetics to expose the class system, its ambiguous ending and its portrait of Eliza made it a permanent part of the repertoire, and its adaptation into My Fair Lady carried it to a world audience.
